requests.purpose: Give the film one generic inspection drone design that leaves its weatherproof station, flies a flight plan between points of interest with an infrared camera, and stands in the window at the close, so the equipment the EPA letter approves is a recognizable object that changes state through the film.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG object in the current Remotion engine. A compact four-rotor inspection drone with a pale gray shell, a slung infrared camera pod with a dark lens, small status lamps, visible rotor discs that blur at speed, short landing legs and a weatherproof charging station with a hinged hood, a pad of worn steel and a leaning post beside it. Late warm desert light from the upper left, cool fill from the right, a soft shadow on the pad. No logos, no brand marks and no real model badge. Maintained but worn, nothing symmetric. A disclosed illustration, never a real drone or station.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of a generic inspection drone and its station. Not a Percepto or Chevron drone, not the approved Air Max, and not a real site, rotor count or flight height.

requests.purpose: Give the drone its world and its records: a Permian well pad with a separator, valves and a tank, a Texas locator, a flight software panel, an approval letter with a date stamp, an illustrated infrared valve, a review panel with an inspector mark and a follow-up tag, a highlighted protocol title, a leak reporting program tag with calendar pages and a proposal tag, and a blank AI box. Keep company attribution visible from the first software frame. Identify the disclosed generic drone with the source-bound Air Max record name and highlight the periodic methane screening scope on the same letter plane.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG support group in the current Remotion engine. A West Texas well pad with a separator vessel, valves, a tank and a pumpjack silhouette on caliche ground, a flat Texas locator with two pins, a software panel with a status row and an blue AI alert flag, an unsealed plain approval letter with worn corners and a crooked date stamp, a gray infrared valve view with a warm illustrative shimmer, a review panel with a certified inspector mark and follow-up tag, a protocol title with a highlighted AI, wall calendar pages, a program tag and an unstamped proposal tag, and a dashed blank AI box. Maintained but worn, nothing symmetric, warm paper against cool gray steel. No agency seal, no logos, no brand marks.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of the sourced records and method. It shows no real site, leak, plume, EPA seal, letter page or person, and the infrared shimmer is not a measured plume.

story_contract.opening_question: When a drone's footage shows a possible leak, who decides it is one?
story_contract.actor: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which approved an Austin company's drone as an alternative method
story_contract.action: Approved the company's autonomous infrared drone for periodic methane screening, with a certified inspector reviewing the footage.
story_contract.change: Methane screening at oil and gas sites can use a drone that flies a flight plan from a station beside the equipment, with a certified inspector still confirming the leak.
story_contract.affected_people: Operators and the certified inspectors who review drone footage and answer a follow-up inspection. No person is named.
story_contract.consequence: A certified inspector's review of the footage identifies any emissions and triggers a follow-up inspection.
story_contract.source_limit: The EPA letter mentions AI only in a protocol title and doesn't say what the AI adds. No source shows Chevron's drone is the approved Air Max, and no Permian site, leak count or repair is published.

documentary.viewer_question: When a drone flags a leak over oil and gas equipment, who decides it is one?
documentary.payoff: The certified inspector mark lands on the footage and outlines the emission, so a person confirms it.
documentary.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of EPA's letter and method. The letter mentions AI only in a protocol title and doesn't say what the AI adds.
documentary.hero_image: A drone following a flight plan to a point of interest and an infrared view of a valve opening.

searches.query: Library of Congress Lyda Hill Texas Collection and press photographs of a Permian Basin well pad, drone station and the Chevron pilot, rights and reuse
searches.finding: The DroneLife article carries press photographs with no reuse licence and no usable Permian well pad photograph was found, so no photograph is admitted.

searches.query: EPA approval letter and MATM-14 method pages for any reusable figure
searches.finding: The letter is text only and its seal may not be reproduced, so the film quotes the sentences by text and draws no seal.

candidates.reason: The page is the source for the Chevron pilot and its photographs have no reuse licence established.

visual_research.decision: No external photograph or footage helps tell this story honestly, so fresh authored illustration performs the sourced method with an Illustration disclosure and no brand marks.

art_direction.palette_reason: Caliche tan carries the Permian pad, galvanized gray steel holds the equipment, warm paper carries the letters and tags, the pale gray of the drone is the one clean value, and a single amber is kept for the alert lamp, stamp and the highlighted AI.
art_direction.shape_language: A compact rounded drone shell against hard rectangular steel vessels, long straight pipe runs and flat paper cards with worn corners. Nothing is symmetric: the post leans, the stamp lands crooked, the highlight overshoots its word.

lighting.motivation: Low warm desert light from the upper left warms the pad, steel and drone shell, cool fill from the right shades the desk scenes, and every grounded thing throws a soft shadow to the right.

hero.silhouette: A compact four-rotor drone with a pale gray shell, a slung infrared camera pod and short legs, sitting in a hooded weatherproof station.
hero.finish: Lit upper-left painted shell with a soft highlight, cool shaded right side, scuffed rotor guards, a dark lens with a small reflection, status lamps and a soft ground shadow on worn steel.

art_direction.focal_hierarchy: The drone or the record first, the inspector mark or the date second, the equipment and the tags third, the pad and the sky last.
art_direction.motion_language: The drone lifts and cruises with continuous acceleration, the route draws at an even speed, cards slide and settle without bounce, stamps and marks land once, and the camera holds while objects perform.

signature_shot.reason: The certified inspector mark lands on the footage and outlines the emission, the whole answer in one movement.

captions.text: In the Permian Basin,
Chevron tested autonomous drones from a company located in Austin.
The companies say AI alerts
when it detects anomalies to normal operations.
On September 30th, 2025,
the Environmental Protection Agency approved
that company's Air Max drone system
for periodic methane screening.
The drone carries an infrared camera
and follows a flight plan to points of interest.
Then a certified inspector reviews the footage
to identify any emissions,
which triggers a follow-up inspection.
The approval letter mentions AI only in the title of a protocol.
EPA also delayed a separate leak reporting program
to January 22nd, 2027,
and on October 7th
said it will propose to rescind it.
Under this approval, a certified inspector confirms the leak.
The letter doesn't say what the AI adds.
